pages.t: A blow with a fly whisk
pages.x: In 1827, in a quarrel over old debts for grain, the ruler of Algiers, the Dey Hussein, struck the French consul with his fly whisk. France blockaded the port. In 1830 the unpopular government of King Charles X, hoping for a victory to win over voters, sent a fleet and 34,000 soldiers to take revenge.

The army landed on the beach at Sidi Fredj in June 1830, beat the Dey's forces and marched on Algiers, which surrendered on 5 July. The Dey sailed into exile, and his treasury was looted. Three weeks later Charles X lost his throne in a revolution in Paris, but France kept Algiers.

In the west, the tribes chose a 24-year-old scholar and horseman, Abdelkader, as their emir in 1832. He built a state of his own around Mascara, with taxes, workshops, schools and a regular army. He beat the French in battle, and in 1837 France made peace, leaving him two thirds of Algeria.

In the east, Ahmed Bey held Constantine, a city on a rock above a deep gorge. A first French attack in 1836 failed in rain and snow. In October 1837 the French came back with heavy guns, blew a breach in the walls and stormed the city street by street.

War broke out again in 1839. In 1841 General Bugeaud took command, with an army that grew to over 100,000 men, and changed the way France fought. Fast columns burned crops, cut down orchards and seized herds, to starve the tribes into giving up. In 1843 French cavalry captured the emir's moving capital of tents, his smala, with thousands of his people.

The king of France ordered a painting of the raid on the smala for his palace at Versailles. Horace Vernet's canvas, finished in 1845, is over 21 metres long, one of the largest paintings in the world: a sea of fleeing women, camels and tents, with the king's son on horseback in the middle.

In 1845 a holy man called Bou Maza led a great revolt in the Dahra mountains. When villagers of the Ouled Riah tribe hid in caves with their animals, Colonel Pélissier had fires lit at the entrance. Hundreds of men, women and children suffocated. The news caused an outcry in France, but Bugeaud defended him.

Abdelkader fought on from Morocco, and in 1845 he wiped out a French column at Sidi Brahim. But France had beaten Morocco in 1844 and made its sultan turn against him. Hunted on both sides of the border, he surrendered in December 1847, on the promise that he could go into exile in a Muslim land.

France broke its promise and kept Abdelkader prisoner until 1852. Freed, he settled in Damascus, where in 1860 he saved thousands of Christians from a massacre. Algeria was made part of France and filled with European settlers, while war, famine and disease took a heavy toll on its people. It won independence only in 1962.
pts: Algiers fell in three weeks in 1830
Seventeen years of war to conquer the interior
